blocks.content:
Debiased Inference for AI-Generated Data
without Gold-Standard Labels:
Identification via Multiple Imperfect Measurements∗
Naoki Egami†
Sooahn Shin‡
Abstract
An increasing number of scholars use AI to measure variables they subsequently include in
downstream analyses. Although AI-measured variables are often analyzed as if observed without
error, ignoring prediction errors in automated measurement leads to substantial bias and invalid
confidence intervals in downstream analyses, even if AI measurement accuracy is high, e.g., above
90%. Existing solutions, such as design-based supervised learni

summary.text: Front matter and abstract for Egami and Shin (MIT), 'Debiased Inference for AI-Generated Data without Gold-Standard Labels: Identification via Multiple Imperfect Measurements' (arXiv:2608.18294v2). Treating AI-measured variables as error-free biases downstream inference even above 90% accuracy, while existing corrections (DSL, PPI) require costly gold-standard labels. The authors propose debiased inference with multiple imperfect measurements (DMM), which combines three or more error-prone AI annotations under conditional independence given the latent true label and observed unit-level features (such as text embeddings), proves consistency and asymptotic normality via semiparametric inference theory, and introduces diagnostics for the conditional independence assumption.

blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
One of the most common applications of AI in the social sciences has been in measurement. Re-
searchers have used AI to measure a wide range of variables, such as sentiment, tone, topics (e.g.,
Gilardi, Alizadeh and Kubli, 2023; Ziems et al., 2024), protests, political violence (e.g., Halterman
and Keith, 2026), and job types (e.g., Hansen et al., 2023), among others. Such measurement tasks
are only the first step. Scholars often use learned measurements as key variables of interest in down-
stream analyses. For example, Pan and Chen (2018) annotate whether each online post accuses
local Chine

summary.text: Section 1 (Introduction) and Related Literature. Motivates how non-random, nonclassical errors in AI/LLM annotations bias downstream social-science regressions and harm replicability, and contrasts gold-standard validation methods (DSL, PPI, MAR-S) with the proposed DMM framework, which uses three or more imperfect proxies without gold-standard labels. Summarizes three main contributions—replacing gold-standard labels via conditional CP decomposition given the latent label and rich unit covariates, general moment-estimator applicability for categorical independent or dependent variables with J >= 3 proxies, and LLM-specific design and diagnostic strategies—before situating DMM relative to the AI-generated data, repeated-measurement identification (Kruskal, Hu, Allman–Matias–Rhodes, Dawid–Skene), and proxy-based causal inference literatures.

blocks.title: The Problem Setting and Existing Approaches
blocks.content:
Scholars often use machine or human annotations to measure key variables of interest that they want
to analyze in downstream analysis. However, as recent papers theoretically and empirically show,
5
ignoring measurement errors in the annotation step can bias downstream inference, even when the
accuracy of the annotation step is high, e.g., more than 90%. For clarity of presentation, we first focus
on settings where an error-prone variable is a binary independent variable in downstream analysis. In
Section 4, we generalize our method to settings where an error-prone variable is a general catego

summary.text: Section 2 opening (The Problem Setting and Existing Approaches). Notes that ignoring measurement error in machine or human annotations biases downstream analysis even when annotation accuracy exceeds 90%, and states that Section 2 and Section 3 first focus on a binary error-prone independent variable before Section 4 generalizes to multicategory independent or dependent variables.

blocks.title: Debiased Inference with Gold-Standard Labels
blocks.content:
More recently, a broad class of methods combines predictions available at scale with a smaller sample
of gold-standard measurements to bias-correct downstream analysis. This class of bias-correction
methods includes design-based supervised learning (DSL; Egami et al., 2023, 2026), prediction-
powered inference (PPI; Angelopoulos et al., 2023), methods reviewed in Ludwig, Mullainathan
and Rambachan (2026), MAR-S (Carlson and Dell, 2025), model-assisted impact analysis (Mozer
and Miratrix, 2023), and the control-variate approach of Katsumata and Yamauchi (2023), among
others. All of these method

summary.text: Section 2.2.3 (Debiased Inference with Gold-Standard Labels). Reviews prediction-and-correction estimators (DSL, PPI, MAR-S) that combine large-scale proxy predictions with a gold-standard validation sample, presenting the cross-fitted doubly robust DSL moment function as a benchmark. Explains that DSL achieves unbiasedness for the oracle moment under a known sampling design without assumptions on LLM error structure, and contrasts the continuum of naive, GSO, and validation-based bias-correction approaches.

blocks.title: Debiased Inference with Multiple Imperfect Measurements
blocks.content:
We now show how to use multiple imperfect labels to perform valid downstream inference without
requiring gold-standard labels.
In particular, building on established results on identification of
latent variables, we use the joint distribution of multiple imperfect labels to recover the unbiased
downstream moment under a conditional independence assumption. In Section 3.1, we begin by
reviewing this classical assumption and then relax it to accommodate modern applications of LLM
annotations. We then discuss nonparametric identification (Section 3.2) and propose a consistent
and asymptotically n

summary.text: Section 3 opening and Section 3.1 (Assumptions). Reviews the classical conditional independence assumption X^(1) _||_ ... _||_ X^(J) | X* from the latent-class literature and explains why it fails when human or LLM annotators share input-driven or prompt-driven error sources. Introduces Assumption 3.1, which conditions on both the latent label X* and observed covariates D-tilde = (D, W, Y)—including task features such as text embeddings or prompt metadata—so misclassification rates can vary across both annotators and units.

Defines the K-fold cross-fitted DMM estimator beta-hat_DMM using out-of-fold nuisance estimates (e.g., via EM or sieve methods) and proves Theorem 3.2: beta-hat_DMM is consistent when J - 1 proxy nuisance models converge (multiple robustness) and root-n asymptotically normal when nuisance errors converge at rate o_p(n^{-1/4}), with a plug-in sandwich variance estimator. blocks.title: Multicategory Labels
blocks.content:
So far we have focused on settings with a binary independent or dependent variable. In this sub-
section, we discuss how our method can be generalized to the multicategory case. The downstream
moment argument extends directly; the main additional challenge lies in identifying a vector of class-
specific bridges under stronger rank and anchoring conditions. For the sake of clear presentation, here
we present our method for a multicategory dependent variable, but an analogous extension applies
to the multicategory latent independent variable setting. As discussed earlier, for causal inference
wi

summary.text: Section 4.2 (Multicategory Labels). Extends DMM to a K*-category latent variable with J >= 3 proxies of potentially differing category counts K_j by defining class-specific bridge functions H_a(Y-tilde, D-tilde) via the left inverse S^+(d) of the conditional measurement matrix S(d) and combining single-proxy bridges into the Neyman-orthogonal robust bridge H^R_a = 3 H_{2,a} - 2 H_{3,a}. Discusses Kruskal rank conditions (3K* >= 2K* + 2 when three proxy groups have full column rank K*), composite proxy grouping when individual proxies have fewer than K* categories, anchoring across all K* classes, and uniform lower bounds on the smallest singular value sigma_min{S_j(d)}.

blocks.title: Designing and Assessing Conditional Independence
blocks.content:
Conditional independence is a structural assumption about the residual errors of the measurements
and is not guaranteed by high predictive accuracy of each imperfect measurement. We therefore
first recommend explicitly designing multiple measurements to make the assumption as plausible as
possible (Section 5.1). We then propose a diagnostic tool for the conditional independence assumption
(Section 5.2). We finally propose a direct test of the assumption and a bias-correction estimator in
a special case when a small amount of validation data is available (Section 5.3).
21
5.1

summary.text: Section 5 opening (Designing and Assessing Conditional Independence). Emphasizes that conditional independence of measurement errors is a structural assumption not guaranteed by high proxy accuracy, and previews the three parts of Section 5: measurement design (Section 5.1), gold-standard-free diagnostics (Section 5.2), and direct testing plus DMM-assisted DSL bias correction when a small validation sample is available (Section 5.3).

blocks.title: Making the Conditional Independence Assumption More Plausible
blocks.content:
The first approach is to judiciously create a conditioning set.
Unlike the traditional conditional
independence assumption that only conditions on the latent variable itself (equation (3.1)), our
method explicitly allows for conditioning on auxiliary input- or annotation-level information Di and
the downstream variables Wi. Therefore, by incorporating rich information about each annotation
task, the proposed method allows for measurement errors to be dependent through task difficulty,
such as text length, complexity, language, writing style, or image quality. More generally, researchers
can in

summary.text: Section 5.1 (Making the Conditional Independence Assumption More Plausible). Recommends three practical strategies for LLM and human annotation designs: (1) enriching the conditioning set D-tilde with input features (text length, style, embeddings, or cross-LLM disagreement scores as task-difficulty proxies); (2) partitioning annotators into G >= 3 conditionally independent groups across distinct model families (e.g., GPT, Claude, open-weight LLMs, and blinded humans) while allowing arbitrary within-group error dependence; and (3) randomizing or recording prompt versions across annotators to prevent prompt-induced error correlation.

blocks.title: Diagnostics Without Gold-Standard Labels
blocks.content:
In most applications, researchers can also conduct a diagnostic test to evaluate the observable impli-
cations of the conditional independence assumption.
With exactly three binary proxies and two latent classes, the unrestricted latent-class model is
generically just identified at each fixed value eD = d: the observed label distribution has 23 −1 = 7
degrees of freedom, equal to the 2J +1 = 7 latent-class and measurement parameters. Consequently,
22
the three-proxy model supplies no generic overidentifying restrictions. With J ≥4 proxies, however,
the number of overidentifying restrictions at

summary.text: Section 5.2 (Diagnostics Without Gold-Standard Labels). Notes that three binary proxies with two latent classes are just-identified (7 degrees of freedom and 7 parameters), whereas J >= 4 proxies yield 2^J - 2J - 2 overidentifying restrictions at each covariate value d. Proposes two gold-standard-free specification diagnostics: goodness-of-fit / conditional moment tests comparing the fitted product-mixture distribution to the empirical joint label distribution, and multiplier-bootstrap stability tests comparing DMM parameter estimates across distinct subsets of three or more proxies.

blocks.title: Testing and Bias-Correction with Small Gold-Standard Data
blocks.content:
When the conditional independence assumption is in serious doubt, it is generally recommended to
collect the gold-standard labels, even for a small amount of data, for two reasons: (a) direct testing of
the conditional independence assumption and (b) bias correction without assuming the conditional
independence assumption.
First, a gold-standard sample permits a direct assessment of the conditional independence as-
sumption. Let R indicate that X∗is observed and let ρ be its known sampling probability, as in
Section 2.
For a subset of labels S with |S| ≥2, conditional independence implies the

summary.text: Section 5.3 (Testing and Bias-Correction with Small Gold-Standard Data). Shows how a small validation sample with known sampling probabilities rho_i enables (1) a direct conditional moment test of zero residual products across proxy subsets given X* = a and D-tilde, and (2) a DMM-assisted DSL estimator that uses the cross-fitted DMM moment function as a full-sample imputation / control variate corrected by inverse-probability-weighted validation residuals, guaranteeing validity even if conditional independence fails while improving precision when DMM is informative.

blocks.title: Simulation and Empirical Validation
blocks.content:
We use simulation studies (Section 6.1) and real-world empirical validation (Section 6.2) to evaluate
DMM. First, a simulation study calibrated based on an empirical study of political advertisements
(Fowler et al., 2021) examines a latent dependent variable under a synthetic data-generating process
that satisfies the conditional independence assumption. This simulation study evaluates the finite-
sample performance of the DMM estimator under the required assumption. Second, an empirical
validation based on Pan and Chen (2018) examines a latent independent variable using LLM anno-
tations. Thi

summary.text: Section 6 opening (Simulation and Empirical Validation). Previews the two empirical evaluations of DMM: a calibrated simulation study of political advertising tone based on Fowler et al. (2021) where conditional independence holds by construction for a latent dependent variable (Section 6.1), and a real-data validation study of online corruption complaints in China based on Pan and Chen (2018) with LLM proxy annotations for a latent independent variable without imposing conditional independence (Section 6.2).

blocks.title: Simulation Study: Platform Differences in Political Advertising Tone
blocks.content:
Fowler et al. (2021) compare the tone of political advertisements on Facebook and television. We use
the expert-coded “Promote” indicator as the latent dependent variable and target the coefficient on
the Facebook indicator in an ad-level logistic regression adjusting for party, incumbency status, and
office type. We hold the observed covariates for 12,973 advertisements fixed and simulate the latent
outcome and proxy label models so that the resulting distributions are similar to the distribution
of the original expert labels and LLM annotations. Please see Section 5 of Egami et al. (2026) fo

summary.text: Section 6.1 (Simulation Study: Platform Differences in Political Advertising Tone). Evaluates DMM over 500 Monte Carlo replications calibrated to 12,973 ads from Fowler et al. (2021), estimating the Facebook coefficient (target 1.314) in a logistic regression for the binary Promote indicator as J increases from 3 to 15 F1-ranked proxies. Reports that with the top 3 proxies naive majority voting suffers severe bias (0.186) and near-zero 95% CI coverage (0.018), whereas DMM eliminates bias (0.002), achieves nominal coverage (0.948), cuts RMSE by two thirds (0.063 vs. 0.191), and approaches the infeasible oracle RMSE (0.045) as informative proxies are added.

blocks.title: Empirical Validation: Accusations of Wrongdoing in China
blocks.content:
Pan and Chen (2018) study whether Chinese officials conceal online complaints that accuse local
officials of wrongdoing. We treat the expert-coded indicator of prefecture-level wrongdoing as the
latent independent variable and upward reporting as the downstream dependent variable. The main
estimand is the coefficient on prefecture-level wrongdoing in a logistic regression of upward reporting
on the latent indicator and a subset of the covariates (7 binary and 1 continuous) used in the original
application. The analysis contains 1,412 complaints and uses the LLM annotations as proxy labels.
We

summary.text: Section 6.2 (Empirical Validation: Accusations of Wrongdoing in China) and Figure 1 captions/labels. Evaluates DMM on 1,412 real citizen complaints from Pan and Chen (2018) using three LLM proxies (GPT-4.1 5-shot, GPT-4 5-shot, Llama-4 0-shot) for the latent prefecture-level wrongdoing regressor in a logistic regression of upward reporting (expert benchmark -1.039). Shows that single-proxy naive estimates are heavily biased (-1.869 to -0.388, coverage 0.154-0.572), while DMM without any expert labels yields -0.844 with 0.862 resample coverage, comparable to DSL using 500 expert labels (-1.279, coverage 0.981).

blocks.title: Discussion
blocks.content:
In this paper, we proposed debiased inference with multiple imperfect measurements (DMM), a
framework to conduct valid downstream inference without gold-standard labels. Under the condi-
tional independence assumption given the latent variable and any observed features of annotation
tasks, such as annotation difficulty, captured by text embeddings, DMM identifies the conditional
classification rate model required for valid downstream inference. Importantly, individual measure-
ments may remain systematically biased, differ substantially in accuracy, and exhibit error rates
that vary across uni

summary.text: Section 7 (Discussion), Figure 2 labels/caption, and References. Synthesizes DMM's methodological contributions—identifying conditional classification rates via covariate-conditioned latent-class decomposition, achieving Neyman orthogonality and single-proxy misspecification robustness via the symmetric bridge H^R, and analyzing how proxy count and quality govern asymptotic variance—alongside its main limitation (reliance on conditional independence) and complementarity with validation-based methods (DSL, PPI), followed by the full bibliography.

summary.text: Appendix B (Details for the Efficiency Discussion). Derives the oracle-plus-bridge-noise decomposition of the DMM meat matrix Omega^R_{0,J} (equations 3.17-3.19) and uses conditional orthogonality of centered single-bridge errors epsilon_j to obtain the exact conditional bridge variance formula v^R_{a,J}(d) in terms of elementary symmetric sums S_{1,a,J}, S_{2,a,J}, and S_{3,a,J} of single-proxy variances kappa_{j,a}(d). Derives the exact variance-reduction threshold kappa-bar_{J,a}(d) for adding a (J+1)-th proxy and shows that under homogeneous proxy variance kappa_a(d), v^R_{a,J}(d) decays at rate O(J^{-2}) and any new proxy with variance below asymptotically 2 kappa_a(d) improves precision.

This appendix provides additional information on the two studies in Section 6. We first clarify how
our analyses relate to the original applications, then describe the logistic latent-class model and the

details. Throughout, an “expert label” denotes the benchmark annotation.

blocks.title: Scope and Relationship to the Original Applications
blocks.content:
The two analyses are numerical illustrations of DMM rather than exact replications of the origi-
nal substantive studies. In the first application, the original analysis and the DSL validation study
examine differences in political-advertising tone between Facebook and television using the original
expert-coded corpus and a candidate-adjusted downstream analysis (Fowler et al., 2021; Egami et al.,
2026). We instead use a transparent ad-level logistic regression for a binary Promote indicator. The
original annotation file contains 13,040 expert-coded ads. After merging it with the platform and

summary.text: Appendix C.1 (Scope and Relationship to the Original Applications). Clarifies how the two Section 6 studies simplify the original empirical specifications to isolate a single latent binary variable: using an ad-level logit on 12,973 complete-case ads without candidate fixed effects for Fowler et al. (2021), and focusing solely on the prefecture-level wrongdoing main effect without county-level wrongdoing interactions on 1,412 complaints for Pan and Chen (2018). Explains the three evaluation roles played by expert labels (oracle benchmark, synthetic DGP calibration, and retrospective F1 ranking of proxy sets).
